shows: The story says that Juneau's water utility did not meet peak demand in the summer 2013 cruise season. Water comes from five wells in Last Chance Basin and from Salmon Creek Reservoir. On average the utility distributes 3.5 million gallons a day; in the summer it can spike to five million gallons a day, and summer 2013 saw those peaks even though cruise ships were limited to a total of 200,000 gallons a day. The peak is 5 / 3.5 = 1.42857 times the average (derived). The water utility superintendent says the system was designed with a capacity of five million gallons a day, and that the wells run up to 23 hours a day because their production has declined. Six cruise ships in port can take about 1 million gallons a day, 20 percent of the summer daily use. Juneau sold about 25 million gallons to cruise ships in 2013; on average ships take about 61 million gallons a year, about 11 percent of the summer production.
limits: A news report that quotes the utility, not a utility record. The figures are rounded and the peak is not a dated, metered day. The 3.5 MGD average has no stated year. The 2013 peak was reached with cruise ship sales held to 200,000 gallons a day, so the unconstrained demand was higher. The design capacity of five million gallons a day is for the 2013 system, before the Salmon Creek filtration plant was built.

quotes.text: Six cruise ships docked in Juneau at once can guzzle about 1 million gallons of water a day. That’s 20 percent of Juneau’s daily water usage in the summer.
But the ships were limited to a total of 200,000 gallons a day this past summer due to unusually hot temperatures and an aging well system.

Juneau’s water supply comes from five wells in Last Chance Basin as well as from Salmon Creek Reservoir. On average, the utility distributes 3.5 million gallons of water a day. In the summer, that number can spike to five million gallons a day.
This recent summer saw those peaks, even with the ships taking a lot less.
Production rates have declined so, as Crabtree explains, the utility keeps the wells running for up to 23 hours a day.
“Just because you design a water system that has the capacity of doing five million gallons a day doesn’t mean you do five million gallons a day every day,”
On average, cruise ships consume about 61 million gallons of Juneau’s water per year, about 11 percent of the city’s total summer production.

locator: Purpose, Current Use, Existing Supply Infrastructure Maintenance items 1 and 4, and Water Supply Expansion Preference
shows: On average, CBJ uses 3.5 to 4.5 MGD, with the higher values in the summer, primarily spurred by sales to cruise ships. Of that volume, Last Chance Basin typically provides 3 to 4 MGD and Salmon Creek 0 to 2 MGD. The Last Chance Basin well field has five wells, 100 to 130 feet deep, and needs only chlorine disinfection; water production capacity has declined in some of the wells. Salmon Creek is an unfiltered, secondary, interruptible surface supply; its chlorine contact tank is designed to treat up to seven MGD, but CBJ typically uses no more than two MGD of it. CBJ has water rights at Salmon Creek for up to 10 MGD and makes beneficial use of up to 2.0 MGD. The plan names increased cruise ship demand as one reason to build a filtration plant at Salmon Creek.
limits: A 2012 draft, before the Salmon Creek filtration plant was built. The 3 to 4 MGD from Last Chance Basin is the typical production of the well field, not a rated capacity, and the plan says some wells have lost capacity. The 3.5 to 4.5 MGD is a seasonal range of average use, not a highest day. The seven MGD is the design of the Salmon Creek contact tank, not what the source supplied.

locator: Page text, paragraphs 1 to 6 and the list of mitigative measures
shows: The Salmon Creek dam and reservoir, owned by AEL&P, provides about one third of the source water of CBJ. From April 1 to June 30 of each year from 2026 to 2029, AEL&P replaces the upper penstock and the flow from the reservoir stops, so CBJ must serve the whole city from a single supply near downtown. Salmon Creek also keeps volume and pressure in the northwest of the city (Lemon Creek, Mendenhall Valley, Auke Lake, Lena). To reduce demand, CBJ plans to stop hydrant use west and northwest of the Salmon Creek facility, to reduce service to industrial consumers at its discretion, and to suspend water supply to commercial cruise ships and other transient vessels during the outage periods.
limits: A plan for a planned outage, with no volumes: it gives the share of Salmon Creek only as about one third and no capacity of the single remaining supply. Undated page.

locator: Original story of Friday, May 9, 2014, and the update of Monday, May 12, 2014
shows: In warm, dry weather in May 2014, CBJ asked residents to conserve water. Salmon Creek had been offline for a week because of turbidity, and the reservoirs were about 30 percent below normal (42 percent of capacity on May 11). The draw on Last Chance Basin late on Friday, May 9 was about 2,100 gallons a minute; the Public Works Director says it was putting out almost 3 million gallons a day, 'pumping for all it's worth'. 2,100 gallons a minute is 3.024 million gallons a day (derived). The city was not selling water to cruise ships. It had plans and funds to build a Salmon Creek filtration plant and to expand Last Chance Basin, both two years away.
limits: A news report that quotes the utility, read through a third-party rendering. The 2,100 gallons a minute is one reading of the well field at full pumping in May 2014, not a rated capacity. It is from before the planned expansion of Last Chance Basin, which may have raised it; no later figure was found. It gives no total demand for the day.

lcb_output_full_pumping.note: Derived: 2,100 gal/min x 1,440 min/day = 3,024,000 gal/day; the director says 'almost 3-million gallons a day'.

The city is not selling water to cruise ships, he says.
